description: Functional properties of proteins and carbohydrates: how heat, acid and mechanical action change food structure.
content_html:
Functional Properties of Proteins

Proteins are not just a nutrient — they are functional ingredients that change their structure when heat, acid or mechanical force is applied. The spec identifies four functional properties of proteins: denaturation, coagulation, gluten formation and foam formation. These four processes underpin almost every baked or cooked protein-rich product, from a Victoria sponge to a quiche Lorraine.

Denaturation

Protein molecules exist in a precise three-dimensional coiled shape, held together by weak chemical bonds. When those bonds are disrupted — by heat, acid, salt or physical beating — the protein unfolds. This is denaturation. Think of the moment a raw egg hits a hot pan: the transparent, runny protein rapidly turns white and opaque as the albumin proteins in the white denature. The process is permanent — you cannot unfry an egg. Acids denature protein too. A lemon juice and olive oil marinade applied to raw salmon begins to denature the surface proteins before any heat is applied. The flesh turns from translucent to opaque, and the texture firms slightly. This is why “ceviche” — raw fish marinated in citrus juice — appears cooked even though no heat has been used.

Coagulation

Once proteins have denatured, continued heating causes them to coagulate: the unfolded chains bond to each other and form a solid, set network. When you bake a quiche, the egg-and-milk custard filling is liquid when it goes into the oven. As the temperature rises above about 70°C, the egg proteins denature and then coagulate, turning the filling from liquid to a solid, sliceable set. Too much heat (or too long in the oven) causes over-coagulation: the protein network contracts, squeezing out water and giving you a rubbery, watery quiche instead of a smooth, creamy one. Temperature control is everything.

Students frequently use these terms interchangeably, but they are two distinct stages. Denaturation is the unfolding of the protein’s shape — the bonds holding the coiled structure are broken and the protein becomes a loose chain. At this point the protein is still a separate molecule. Coagulation only happens afterwards: the loose, denatured chains start bonding to each other, forming a new cross-linked solid structure. So denaturation must happen first; coagulation is what follows. Think of it as “unravel, then re-join”. A 4-mark Explain question may specifically ask you to sequence these two stages — if you confuse them or call them the same process, you will lose marks.

Gluten Formation

Wheat flour contains two proteins: glutenin and gliadin. Individually, these proteins are relatively inert. But add water and work the mixture — kneading bread dough, rubbing fat into flour for pastry, mixing a cake batter — and these proteins combine to form gluten, an elastic network of long, stretchy strands. Gluten is what traps the carbon dioxide released by yeast in bread-making, allowing the dough to rise. The more you knead, the stronger and more elastic the gluten network becomes. This is why bread dough needs ten minutes of vigorous kneading to develop its full structure, while shortcrust pastry is handled as little as possible — you want a crumbly, short texture, not a tough, chewy one. Over-mixing pastry develops too much gluten and makes the final result tough.

Foam Formation

When egg whites are whisked vigorously, air is beaten into the liquid. The albumin proteins in the egg white are denatured by the mechanical action and form a thin, stable film around each air bubble. The result is a foam — a gas-in-liquid system where air is the gas and the egg white is the liquid. As you continue whisking, more and more air is incorporated until the foam reaches soft-peak stage, then stiff-peak stage. At stiff peak, the foam holds its shape. In a whisked sponge, the foam is folded into the batter; the trapped air expands in the oven, giving the cake its light texture. Over-whisking eventually breaks the protein film and the foam collapses — the egg white turns grainy and watery.

Key Fact

Four functional properties of proteins: denaturation (egg turns opaque in a hot pan); coagulation (quiche custard sets on baking); gluten formation (elastic dough develops when wheat flour is kneaded with water); foam formation (whisked egg whites trap air for a whisked sponge).

Functional Properties of Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates, especially starches and sugars, also have key functional properties that affect cooking outcomes. The spec identifies three: gelatinisation, dextrinisation and caramelisation. These three are frequently confused with each other in the exam — precise vocabulary is essential.

Gelatinisation

When starch granules are mixed with a cold liquid, they remain intact and separate. As the mixture is heated above about 60°C, the granules begin to absorb liquid and swell. Around 85°C they burst, releasing starch molecules that tangle together and thicken the liquid into a gel — this is gelatinisation. A roux-based béchamel sauce begins as butter and flour cooked together into a paste; when warm milk is added and the mixture is heated with constant stirring, the starch granules in the flour swell and burst, and the sauce thickens. The amount of starch added relative to the liquid controls the final viscosity: a thick pouring sauce uses less starch; a very stiff sauce or a setting agent uses more. This ratio is critical in sauce making.

Dextrinisation

Dextrinisation happens when starch on the surface of food is heated in dry conditions to above about 110°C. The starch breaks down into shorter molecules called dextrins, which are brown, have a toasted flavour and are partly soluble. The golden-brown crust on a loaf of bread is the result of dextrinisation: the starch in the outer layer of the dough is exposed to the dry heat of the oven and browns. Toast is an even clearer example — the pale bread surface goes from white to golden-brown to dark as the starch progressively dextrinises. This is not the same as the Maillard reaction, which involves both sugars and amino acids; dextrinisation involves starch only.

Caramelisation

Caramelisation occurs when sugars — not starch — are heated above approximately 160°C. The sugar molecules break down and recombine into hundreds of new compounds that produce shades of amber and brown, and a range of flavours from sweet and nutty to slightly bitter. Sprinkle sugar over a crème brûlée and apply a blowtorch: the sucrose melts and then caramelises into a hard, glass-like sheet. Roasted parsnips or carrots also caramelise where their natural sugars are exposed to the high, dry heat of an oven, which is why they develop a sweet, brown, almost sticky surface. Caramelisation requires higher temperatures than gelatinisation or dextrinisation and only involves sugars.

These three processes are routinely confused on the written paper. Here is the key to telling them apart:

Gelatinisation: starch + liquid + heat (60–80°C+) → granules swell and burst → mixture thickens. The ingredient is starch; the medium is water; the result is a gel or thick sauce.

Dextrinisation: starch + dry heat (110°C+) → starch breaks down to dextrins → brown colour and toasted flavour. The ingredient is starch; there is NO water; the result is surface browning (bread crust, toast).

Caramelisation: sugar + dry heat (160°C+) → sugar breaks down → brown colour and caramel flavour. The ingredient is sugar (not starch); there is NO water; the result is sweet, brown colour (crème brûlée top, roasted carrots).

Key Fact

Gelatinisation: starch granules absorb liquid and swell above 60°C, burst around 85°C, releasing starch molecules that tangle and thicken the liquid. Starch-to-liquid ratio controls viscosity — more starch gives a thicker result.
exam_tip_html: A very common error on questions about functional properties is attaching the wrong term to the wrong food group. Gelatinisation, dextrinisation and caramelisation belong to carbohydrates; denaturation, coagulation, gluten formation and foam formation belong to proteins. Mixing these up is one of the most frequent mark-losing mistakes on this topic. When the command word is Describe, the marker wants three distinct, characterised points — not just a list of terms. For example, if asked to describe what happens during gelatinisation, ‘starch granules swell’ is one point, not three. You need: the granules absorb liquid and swell (1); above a higher temperature they burst (1); the released starch molecules tangle and thicken the liquid into a gel (1). On a 9-mark Analyse question, you would also examine the role of the starch-to-liquid ratio and how agitation prevents lumps — breaking the process into parts and examining the relationships between variables is what ‘Analyse’ demands.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Proteins have four functional properties: denaturation (unfolding), coagulation (bonding and setting), gluten formation (elastic network in wheat flour) and foam formation (air trapped by protein film in whisked egg whites) — each stage is distinct and sequential where denaturation precedes coagulation.
  • Carbohydrates have three functional properties: gelatinisation (starch swells and bursts in liquid above 60°C, thickening sauces), dextrinisation (starch browns in dry heat above 110°C, forming bread crust) and caramelisation (sugars brown in dry heat above 160°C, giving sweet, amber colour).
  • The starch-to-liquid ratio controls viscosity in gelatinisation; over-mixing develops too much gluten in pastry; and over-whisking collapses a foam — process control determines the final outcome in each case.

practice_questions.text:
Which term describes the process in which denatured protein chains bond together and solidify on continued heating?
A. Gelatinisation
B. Dextrinisation
C. Coagulation
D. Foam formation
Name the two proteins in wheat flour that combine to form gluten when water is added.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for glutenin; 1 mark for gliadin.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to starch granules during gelatinisation.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: the starch granules absorb liquid and begin to swell as temperature rises above approximately 60 degrees C (1); above approximately 85 degrees C the granules burst, releasing starch molecules into the liquid (1); the released starch molecules tangle together and thicken the mixture into a gel (1).

practice_questions.text: Niamh is making shortcrust pastry for a quiche. Her teacher tells her the pastry should be handled as little as possible. Explain why over-working the pastry dough would make the finished result tough rather than crumbly.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: wheat flour contains two proteins, glutenin and gliadin (1); when water is added and the dough is worked, these combine to form gluten (1); the more the dough is kneaded or worked, the stronger and more elastic the gluten network becomes (1); a strong gluten network makes the pastry tough and chewy rather than short and crumbly, because the protein strands have bonded extensively and resist breaking apart (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the functional properties of both starch and egg protein work together to produce a smooth, set quiche filling, and explain what happens when the quiche is overbaked.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): Accurate identification and explanation of gelatinisation (starch from any flour or thickener in the filling absorbs liquid and helps create a smooth gel texture) and protein coagulation (egg protein denatures then coagulates when heated, setting the custard filling); clear analysis of how these two processes work together (the starch and egg protein both contribute to structure, each playing a different role); clear analysis of the effect of overbaking (over-coagulation causes protein network to contract, expelling water, giving rubbery, watery, shrunken filling; also over-heating starch can break down the gel structure); accurate food-science vocabulary throughout; sustained reasoning linking cause to effect.
Secure (5-7 marks): Correct identification of both gelatinisation and coagulation with some explanation; some analysis of overbaking effects; vocabulary mostly accurate; some but not full examination of the relationships between the two processes.
Developing (3-4 marks): One of the two processes well-described; some mention of the other; limited analysis of overbaking or only descriptive.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic relevant points only, e.g. 'egg sets on heating' with no further development.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between dextrinisation and caramelisation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each valid difference (any two from): dextrinisation involves starch; caramelisation involves sugars; dextrinisation occurs above approximately 110 degrees C, caramelisation above approximately 160 degrees C (so caramelisation needs a higher temperature); dextrinisation produces a toasted/bread crust flavour, caramelisation produces a sweet/nutty/bitter caramel flavour; examples: dextrinisation gives bread its brown crust; caramelisation gives creme brulee its glassy top or roasted vegetables their sweet surface.

knowledge_checks.q: When egg whites are whisked, a foam forms. What is the correct scientific description of this foam?
options: A liquid-in-gas system where egg white droplets are suspended in air.
A gas-in-liquid system where air bubbles are trapped by a protein film.
A solid-in-liquid system formed by coagulated albumin proteins.
A gel formed by gelatinisation of egg-white starch.

knowledge_checks.q: Which process is responsible for the golden-brown crust that forms on the surface of a loaf of bread during baking?
options: Caramelisation of the sugar in the flour
Coagulation of gluten proteins at the surface
Gelatinisation of starch in the presence of steam
Dextrinisation of surface starch in dry oven heat

knowledge_checks.q: In wheat flour, the proteins glutenin and gliadin combine with water and mechanical working to form _____, an elastic network that traps gas in bread dough.
Once a protein has denatured and continued heating causes the unfolded chains to bond together and solidify, this second stage is called _____.
Match each carbohydrate functional property to the correct food example.
right: Sugar heated on a creme brulee turns amber and glass-like
Starch granules in a bechamel sauce burst and thicken the milk
Surface starch on toast browns in dry heat

flashcard_questions.q: What is denaturation in a protein?
flashcard_questions.a: The unfolding of a protein's 3D structure by heat, acid or mechanical action.

flashcard_questions.q: What is coagulation in a protein?
flashcard_questions.a: Denatured protein chains bond together and solidify on continued heating.

flashcard_questions.q: Which comes first — denaturation or coagulation?
flashcard_questions.a: Denaturation always comes first; coagulation follows.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the two proteins in wheat flour that form gluten.
Why must shortcrust pastry be handled as little as possible?
flashcard_questions.a: Over-working develops too much gluten, making the pastry tough.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of system is a whisked egg-white foam?
flashcard_questions.a: A gas-in-liquid foam — air bubbles trapped by a protein film.
Starch granules absorb liquid, swell and burst above 60 degrees C, thickening the mixture.

flashcard_questions.q: What controls the thickness (viscosity) of a gelatinised sauce?
flashcard_questions.a: The ratio of starch to liquid — more starch gives a thicker result.
Starch breaks down to dextrins in dry heat above 110 degrees C, browning the surface.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one food example of dextrinisation.
flashcard_questions.a: The golden-brown crust on a baked loaf of bread.
Sugars break down in dry heat above 160 degrees C, producing brown colour and complex flavour.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one food example of caramelisation.
flashcard_questions.a: The glassy amber top of a creme brulee when a blowtorch is applied.

flashcard_questions.q: A quiche filling is overbaked and turns rubbery. What has gone wrong at a molecular level?
flashcard_questions.a: Over-coagulation — the protein network contracts and expels water.

flashcard_questions.q: How does an acid marinade begin to change raw fish or meat before cooking?
flashcard_questions.a: The acid denatures surface proteins, firming the texture and allowing flavours to penetrate.

glossary_terms.definition: The unfolding of a protein's coiled three-dimensional structure caused by heat, acid, salt or mechanical action, changing its shape permanently without breaking it apart.
The process by which denatured proteins bond together and solidify on continued heating, setting the structure of the food.
The development of an elastic network of gluten proteins (glutenin and gliadin) in wheat flour dough when water is added and the dough is kneaded or worked.
A gas-in-liquid system in which air bubbles are trapped and held by a protein film around each bubble, as in whisked egg whites.
The process in which starch granules absorb liquid, swell and eventually burst when heated above approximately 60 degrees C, thickening the mixture as the starch molecules form a gel.
The browning reaction that occurs when starch on the surface of a food is heated in dry conditions above 110 degrees C, breaking down the starch and producing brown, flavoursome compounds.
The browning reaction that occurs when sugars are heated above approximately 160 degrees C without proteins present, producing brown colour and complex, sweet, slightly bitter flavour compounds.
